clinicalPearls: A malignant trophoblastic tumour that most often follows a molar pregnancy but can arise after any pregnancy event, including miscarriage, ectopic, or term delivery
Persistent or irregular vaginal bleeding after a pregnancy, with a markedly elevated beta-hCG, is the hallmark presentation
It is highly vascular and prone to early haematogenous spread, classically to the lungs, but also brain, liver, and pelvis
Presenting features may reflect metastasis, such as haemoptysis, neurological signs, or intraperitoneal bleeding, rather than a gynaecological complaint
Beta-hCG functions as a sensitive tumour marker for diagnosis, monitoring response, and detecting relapse
Management is methotrexate-based or multi-agent chemotherapy guided by a validated prognostic scoring system, delivered through a specialist trophoblastic centre
Even with widespread metastatic disease, cure rates are high with appropriate risk-stratified chemotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Choriocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm of trophoblast composed of sheets of anaplastic cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast without formed chorionic villi. It arises from residual trophoblastic tissue after a molar or non-molar pregnancy, secreting beta-hCG in proportion to tumour bulk. The tumour destructively invades the myometrium and uterine vasculature, causing haemorrhage, and disseminates early through the bloodstream to distant organs where friable vascular deposits may bleed. Because it is chemosensitive, systemic chemotherapy can eradicate even metastatic disease, with beta-hCG tracking the response.
additionalDifferentials: Retained products of conception with exaggerated placental site
Non-gestational germ cell tumour producing hCG
additionalInvestigations: Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler to assess uterine mass and vascularity
Chest imaging to detect pulmonary metastases
Cross-sectional imaging of brain, liver, and abdomen for staging in high-risk disease
Full blood count, renal and liver function before chemotherapy
Histology when tissue is available, though treatment often begins on hCG and imaging
redFlags: Haemoptysis or breathlessness suggesting pulmonary metastases
Headache, seizures, or focal neurology indicating cerebral spread
Acute intraperitoneal or vaginal haemorrhage from a friable tumour
Very high beta-hCG with widespread metastatic disease requiring urgent specialist chemotherapy
reference.prognosis: Gestational choriocarcinoma is one of the most curable solid malignancies; low-risk disease is almost uniformly cured and even high-risk metastatic disease achieves high survival with multi-agent chemotherapy through a specialist centre. Prognosis worsens with late presentation, very high hCG, and brain or liver metastases.
pitfalls: Overlooking abnormal bleeding weeks or months after a normal-appearing pregnancy and not checking beta-hCG
Attempting biopsy of a highly vascular uterine lesion and precipitating major haemorrhage
Managing outside a specialist trophoblastic service and undertreating high-risk disease
Discontinuing chemotherapy or surveillance before beta-hCG has normalised and been sustained
references: RCOG guidance on gestational trophoblastic disease
FIGO gestational trophoblastic neoplasia staging and scoring
management: Refer to a specialist gestational trophoblastic disease centre, with treatment intensity set by a validated prognostic scoring system
Treat low-risk disease with single-agent chemotherapy such as methotrexate with folinic acid rescue or actinomycin D
Treat high-risk or metastatic disease with multi-agent chemotherapy such as the EMA-CO regimen
Track response, guide treatment duration and detect relapse with serial quantitative beta-hCG measurement
Manage haemorrhagic and metastatic complications, adding radiotherapy or surgery for chemoresistant or bleeding deposits such as cerebral metastases
Advise reliable contraception throughout treatment and surveillance, avoiding pregnancy until beta-hCG has remained normal for the recommended interval
Provide prolonged post-treatment beta-hCG surveillance to confirm remission and detect recurrence
